(a) Limitation.—Of the funds authorized to be appropriated by this Act or otherwise made available for fiscal year 2013 for the Air Force for the evolved expendable launch vehicle program, 10 percent may not be obligated or expended until the date on 
which the Secretary of the Air Force submits to the appropriate congressional committees—
        (1) a report describing the acquisition strategy for such program; and 
        (2) written certification that such strategy—
            (A) maintains assured access to space; 
            (B) achieves substantial cost savings; and 
            (C) provides opportunities for competition.   
    (b) Matters Included.—The report under subsection (a)(1) shall include the following information:
        (1) The anticipated savings to be realized under the acquisition strategy for the evolved expendable launch vehicle program. 
        (2) The number of launch vehicle booster cores covered by the planned contract for such program. 
        (3) The number of years covered by such contract. 
        (4) An assessment of when new entrants that have submitted a statement of intent will be certified to compete for evolved expendable launch vehicle-class launches. 
        (5) The projected launch manifest, including possible opportunities for certified new entrants to compete for evolved expendable launch vehicle-class launches. 
        (6) Any other relevant analysis used to inform the acquisition strategy for such program.  
    (c) Comptroller General.—
        (1) Review.—The Comptroller General of the United States shall review the report under subsection (a)(1). 
        (2) Submittal.—Not later than 30 days after the date on which the report under subsection (a)(1) is submitted to the appropriate congressional committees, the Comptroller General shall—
            (A) submit to such committees a report on the review under paragraph (1); or 
            (B) provide to such committees a briefing on such review.   
    (d) Appropriate Congressional Committees Defined.—In this section, the term “appropriate congressional committees” means the following:
        (1) The congressional defense committees. 
        (2) The Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence of the House of Representatives and the Select Committee on Intelligence of the Senate.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the report-and-certification process, the Comptroller General review, and the references to "new entrants" and "opportunities for competition" amount to outside involvement. But every actor in the process (the Secretary of the Air Force, the congressional committees, the Comptroller General) is inside the federal government, and competing for launch contracts is not participation in a federal decision. The section provides no public comment, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to sue.

opus.w: The section limits funds until the Air Force reports to and certifies to congressional committees, and then has the Comptroller General review the report and brief those same committees. All of these actors are inside the federal government. The mention of new entrants competing for launches only describes what the report must contain. It concerns contract competition, not outside parties being consulted on the decision, so it is not participation.

opus.b:
**Step 1, reasoning:** The tempting reading is that the section involves outsiders, because it mentions "new entrants that have submitted a statement of intent" and "opportunities for competition." Those commercial launch providers are only described as content of the report. They are bidders for contracts, which counts as an application, not participation. They play no consultative role in the acquisition-strategy decision. Every actor here is federal: the Secretary of the Air Force, the congressional committees, and the Comptroller General (GAO). So the section reports to Congress and gets a review inside the government, and nothing crosses the federal boundary.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary of the Air Force to submit a report and certification to congressional committees before obligating funds. Congress and its committees are part of the federal government, so this interaction is internal. The Comptroller General is also a federal official. There is no requirement to consult or coordinate with any party outside the federal government (such as states, tribes, or the public).
qwen_chat.s: the Secretary of the Air Force submits to the appropriate congressional committees
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for the Secretary to submit a report to Congress involves "participation" because it is a procedural step before funds can be used. However, the definition explicitly states that reports to Congress are "inside the federal government" and thus do not count as participation. The Comptroller General is also a federal officer. There is no mention of consulting with states, tribes, the public, or other outside entities.
